clue.text: So, Christmas Eve I prepared a label (3,7,5)

indicators.note: Something prepared has been worked over before it is served, so these letters arrive in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fifteen letters

annotation.surface: Getting a label ready on Christmas Eve.
annotation.walkthrough: The label is a record company rather than something stuck on a parcel, and the trademark behind it is the painting of a terrier listening at a gramophone horn.
annotation.definitionFit: His Master's Voice was the record label named after that painting, and 'label' is the trade's own word for a record company.

clue.text: Cut short elephantine part 8 in report (8)

indicators.note: In report means as it is spoken and passed on, so both pieces are to be heard rather than read.

blocks.note: The part that hangs from an elephant's face; said aloud, that noise is spelt with a C when it runs into what follows.
The numeral spoken aloud is the same noise as the past tense of eat.

annotation.surface: An elephant section, item 8, being cut out of a report.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are heard rather than spelt: an animal's nose and a numeral, run together at speaking speed. 'Report' is the spoken kind, and it is the only word telling you to listen.
annotation.definitionFit: To truncate something is to cut it short by lopping off its end and leaving it incomplete.

clue.text: Giant conger-eel regularly picked out (4)

indicators.note: Letters picked regularly are taken at an even spacing, here every second one, rather than chosen to suit.

blocks.note: Every second letter of the hyphenated run, counting from the second.

annotation.surface: A huge conger eel singled out of the catch.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen only holds the surface together; the count runs straight through it and ignores where one word stops. 'Regularly' is the standard signal for an even step, and the step here is two.
annotation.definitionFit: An ogre is the man-eating giant of folk tales, so the plain noun 'giant' names what it is.

clue.text: Approving British novelist Doris (8)

blocks.note: B is the standard abbreviation for British.
Doris Lessing, the British novelist who won the Nobel prize in 2007.

annotation.surface: A nod of approval for the British novelist Doris.
annotation.walkthrough: Doris Lessing is the Doris the clue wants, and her surname supplies seven of the eight letters. 'Approving' sits where it looks like an adjective describing her, and it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Blessing a plan is approving it: both verbs mean giving something your sanction, and both are in the -ing form here.

clue.text: Amorous prof’s heart captured by upright quote (6)

indicators.note: The heart of a word is its middle, and a four-letter word has two letters sitting there.
Something captured is held inside its captor, so these letters end up enclosed by the other piece.
In a down entry, standing upright means reading from the bottom of the grid towards the top, so that piece arrives the other way round.

blocks.note: To quote a source is to cite it, and those four letters then climb the grid.
The middle two of the four letters.

annotation.surface: A professor's heart won over by a line of poetry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heart' asks for the middle of the word 'prof' itself, not for anybody's feelings. The citation is stood on its end before it wraps round, so the two steps happen in that order.
annotation.definitionFit: Erotic describes what is charged with sexual love, the warmer end of the range that amorous covers.

clue.text: What may connect means of opening crucial calls (3,5)

definitions.text: What may connect means of opening

blocks.note: The crucial detail is the key detail.
To call someone on the phone is to ring them.

annotation.surface: Whatever links the ways of getting through those all-important calls.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition runs five words deep and describes the object instead of naming it, which leaves only 'crucial calls' as wordplay. Both of those words have a second sense doing the real work.
annotation.definitionFit: A keyring is the hoop that threads keys — the means of opening doors — onto one loop so they travel together.

clue.text: Goddess passing through Africa then Asia (6)

indicators.note: Something passing through a place crosses it without stopping, which is how these letters run: unbroken and in order.

blocks.note: Six consecutive letters spanning the gaps between the three words.

annotation.surface: A goddess making her way from Africa on into Asia.
annotation.walkthrough: Two continents and a joining word read as a travel itinerary, and the letters simply cross them. Capital letters mark where the words begin; the run pays no attention to them.
annotation.definitionFit: Athena is the Greek goddess of wisdom and warfare, so the bare word names the class she belongs to.

clue.text: Stuff overturning tired victory changed decisive decision (8,7)

indicators.note: Something overturned is tipped onto its head, so those three letters are read the other way about.
Letters described as changed do not keep the arrangement they came in.

blocks.note: To stuff something into a gap is to jam it in, and those three letters are then turned about.
anagram fodder, twelve letters

annotation.surface: A weary win being overturned, and the ruling that settles it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' is the verb to jam, not the noun the surface offers. Overturning acts on those three letters alone, while 'changed' shuffles the twelve that follow, so two instructions run side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: A majority verdict is the jury's ruling carried by most of its members rather than all of them, and it decides the case.

clue.text: Disorderly soldier pursues international resistance (9)

indicators.note: To pursue is to come along behind, so the soldier's letters follow the two that are already in place.

blocks.note: I is the standard abbreviation for international.
R is the physicist's symbol for resistance.
A regular is a full-time professional soldier, as against a reservist.

annotation.surface: A scruffy soldier chasing after international opposition.
annotation.walkthrough: The soldier chases, so his word lands last though he is named first. A regular soldier and a disorderly one are opposites in the army's own vocabulary, and the clue builds one out of the other.
annotation.definitionFit: Something irregular breaks the settled order or pattern, which is what disorderly says of behaviour and of troops alike.

clue.text: Additional paintings returned by former partner (5)

indicators.note: Something returned comes back the way it went, so in an across entry those letters read from the right.

blocks.note: An ex is the partner you used to have.
Paintings are art, and those three letters come back on themselves.

annotation.surface: Some further canvases sent back by an ex.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Returned' does two jobs at once: sending the pictures back in the story and reversing three letters in the wordplay. The former partner arrives first in the grid though last in the sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: An extra helping is an additional one, the adjective standing in front of a noun exactly as 'additional' does.

clue.text: Social conduct of married princess extremely rigorous (7)

definitions.note: Manners is a plural noun naming a single thing — the whole of a person's behaviour — so it answers an uncountable phrase like 'social conduct'.

indicators.note: The extremes of a word are its two ends, so this asks for the first and last letters and nothing between.

blocks.note: M is the standard abbreviation for married.
Princess Anne, the Princess Royal, is the crossword's usual princess.
The two ends of the word, first letter and last.

annotation.surface: The way a married princess behaves, held to the strictest standard.
annotation.walkthrough: Royal first names are small change in cryptics, and Anne is the one that fits four letters. 'Extremely' looks like it is intensifying 'rigorous' and is in fact picking that word's two ends.
annotation.definitionFit: Manners are the customs of polite behaviour towards other people, which is what social conduct amounts to.

clue.text: Roped to abandoned wreck (7)

indicators.note: Abandoned behaviour is unrestrained, and letters let loose like that will not keep to their order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: A derelict hulk with a rope still attached to it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' reads as derelict, which is what the wreck invites, and means unrestrained. The definition is the last word and it is a verb: sinking a plan as surely as a ship.
annotation.definitionFit: To torpedo a scheme is to wreck it outright, the verb borrowed from the weapon that sinks ships.

clue.text: Fake suntan primarily associated with awful actor (4)

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes first, so only the opening letter of that word is wanted.

blocks.note: The opening letter of the word.
A ham is an actor who overplays every line.

annotation.surface: A fake tan mostly linked with a bad actor.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' reads as 'mainly' in the sentence and is an instruction to take a single letter. Ham for a bad actor is standard crossword currency, from the hammy overacting of the old stage.
annotation.definitionFit: A sham is something got up to pass for the real thing, which is what a fake is.

clue.text: Supreme commander in Nato almost back in Miami, a US city (10)

indicators.note: Almost the whole word means the whole word bar its last letter, stopping just short of the end.
The back of a word is the letter at its rear, the final one.

blocks.note: CINC is the services' shorthand for a commander-in-chief.
The clue's own word, taken exactly as it stands.
The alliance's name minus its last letter, as 'almost' asks.
The last letter of the Florida city's name.

annotation.surface: A Nato supreme commander nearly home again in Miami.
annotation.walkthrough: Four pieces, and the hardest to see is the bare 'in', which is simply itself. 'Back in Miami' sounds like a homecoming and asks for one letter, the one at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Cincinnati is a city in southern Ohio, on the Kentucky border, so 'a US city' names one of many.

clue.text: Latter part of day still boring after halfway mark (7)

indicators.note: Everything after a word's halfway mark is its back half, so the front half is dropped.

blocks.note: Still better and even better say the same thing.
The back half of the six-letter word.

annotation.surface: A dull day that has not picked up since the halfway point.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boring' describes nothing here: it is a six-letter word to be cut in half. 'Still' is wanted in its 'even better' sense, the one that means yet more rather than motionless.
annotation.definitionFit: The evening is the last stretch of the day, running from late afternoon until night.

clue.text: Broke entire shell of hard nuts (2,3,3)

indicators.note: A shell is the hard outside of a thing, so only the outermost letters are taken.
Nuts means crazy, and letters gone crazy will not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
The outside of the word, its first letter and its last.

annotation.surface: Cracking the whole shell off a handful of tough nuts.
annotation.walkthrough: The shell comes off 'hard' first, leaving two letters to join the shuffle. 'Broke' at the front is the money sense, not the past tense of break that the nutshells invite.
annotation.definitionFit: To be in the red is to have an overdrawn account — red was the bank's ink for a negative balance — which is what broke means.

clue.text: Critics ultimately coming in to sink amateur show (7)

indicators.note: What comes ultimately comes at the very end, so it is that word's last letter.
A thing coming in arrives inside, so this letter is placed within the piece it joins rather than beside it.

blocks.note: To sink below the surface is to dip.
The last letter of Critics.
A lay member of a profession is an amateur, as in lay preacher.

annotation.surface: Reviewers turning up at the last minute to sink an amateur production.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sink' is what critics do to a show and is also a three-letter word to be broken open. 'Lay' for amateur comes from the church, where a layman holds no office.
annotation.definitionFit: A display is a show: goods, skills or feelings put out where they can be seen.

clue.text: Stupor consuming one top politician that’s swallowed a tranquillizer (8)

indicators.note: To consume is to take something right inside you, so the stupor closes around what follows it.
What is swallowed goes inside the swallower, so that letter sits within the politician's two.

blocks.note: A daze is the stupor someone is left in.
I is the Roman numeral for one.
PM is the prime minister, the politician at the top.
The clue's own single letter, taken as it stands.

annotation.surface: A prime minister sunk in a stupor, having swallowed something calming.
annotation.walkthrough: Two separate swallowings, one in each half of the answer: the stupor takes a letter and the politician takes another. Nothing in the sentence hints at a pill until the final word.
annotation.definitionFit: Diazepam, sold as Valium, is the benzodiazepine prescribed to calm anxiety, which makes it a tranquillizer.

clue.text: Free beer 50% of Italians brewed (8)

indicators.note: Half of the word's letters are wanted, and with eight to divide that is the first four.
Brewing stirs its ingredients together until nothing is where it started.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters
The first four of its eight letters.

annotation.surface: Free beer that half the Italians brewed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Free' sits at the front looking like the price of the beer, and it is the definition, a verb. 'Brewed' is the shuffle instruction, picked so the surface never gives itself away.
annotation.definitionFit: To liberate prisoners or a city is to free them, the two verbs interchangeable in that sense.

clue.text: Proudly exhibit damn budgie smugglers? (10)

definitions.note: The definition is a plural example rather than a synonym: one kind of garment standing in for the whole category, which the question mark flags.

blocks.note: To sport a new hat is to wear it where everyone can see it.
To damn something is to swear at it.

annotation.surface: Someone showing off a pair of very tight swimming trunks.
annotation.walkthrough: Budgie smugglers is Australian slang for men's brief swimming trunks, tight enough to look like smuggled livestock. 'Damn' is the verb, an oath sworn rather than the exclamation the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: Budgie smugglers, the Australian name for tight swimming trunks, are one kind of sportswear, and the question mark admits it is an example.

clue.text: Alternative point breaks hearts of spoilt baronets (6)

indicators.note: To break into something is to force a way inside, so these letters split the piece they land in.
The heart of a word is its middle, and each of these words has an even number of letters, so two come out of each.

blocks.note: The middle two of its six letters.
The middle two of its eight letters.
PT is the standard abbreviation for point.

annotation.surface: A rival argument breaking the hearts of pampered young baronets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hearts' means the middles of two words, not anybody's feelings, and the abbreviation is dropped into the first pair. A baronet is the lowest hereditary British title, a Sir who is not a lord.
annotation.definitionFit: An option is one of the choices open to you, which is exactly what an alternative is.

clue.text: Rings after start of weekend – my mistake (6)

indicators.note: 'After' sends the rings in behind, so the single letter named next is the one that comes first.
The start of a word is its opening letter.

blocks.note: The first letter of weekend.
Rings you toss over a peg are hoops.

annotation.surface: Phone calls once the weekend has started, and an apology.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash does the work of a colon: everything before it builds, everything after it defines. 'Rings' are the fairground kind, though the surface is offering telephones.
annotation.definitionFit: Whoops is the noise you make on dropping something, the spoken equivalent of owning up with 'my mistake'.

clue.text: Gong smothers old instrument (4)

indicators.note: To smother something is to cover it over entirely, so these letters close around what they cover.

blocks.note: A gong is British slang for a medal, and the OBE — Order of the British Empire — is the commonest one handed out.
O is the standard abbreviation for old.

annotation.surface: A medal laid over an old instrument.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gong' is the medal, not the thing you strike, which is the whole trick in a four-letter clue that ends on the word 'instrument'. British slang has called an honour a gong since the 1920s.
annotation.definitionFit: An oboe is a double-reed woodwind, so 'instrument' names the family it belongs to.

clue.text: Busy month egocentric nails (2,3,2)

indicators.note: To nail something is to fix it firmly in place, and these letters are held in position inside the words, in the order they are given.

blocks.note: Seven consecutive letters spanning the join between the two words.

annotation.surface: A self-centred type sailing through a busy month.
annotation.walkthrough: The join between the two words is where the letters cross, and nobody reads across a space, which is what makes a long concealment hard to spot. 'Nails' is the instruction, in its pinning-down sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone on the go is constantly busy, never settled in one place for long.

clue.text: Electrician’s first dodgy tender came in (7)

indicators.note: The first of a word is its opening letter.
Something dodgy cannot be trusted to be what it seems, and nor can the order these letters come in.

blocks.note: The opening letter of Electrician.
anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: An electrician's shady bid for the job arriving.
annotation.walkthrough: A tender is a written bid for a contract, which keeps the surface inside the trade. The definition is the two words at the end, a past tense the answer has to match.
annotation.definitionFit: To have entered a room is to have come in, and both are in the past tense.

clue.text: Remote partly turned up volume (4)

indicators.note: Only part of the word is wanted, and that part is a run of letters sitting inside it.
In a down entry, letters turned up are read from the bottom of the grid towards the top, so they arrive the other way round.

blocks.note: Four letters sitting together inside the word, with one spare at each end.

annotation.surface: Turning the remote up to raise the volume.
annotation.walkthrough: The volume is a book, not the loudness the remote control invites. The letters sit inside a single word and are then read back up the grid, so two things happen to them.
annotation.definitionFit: A tome is a big, heavy book — one volume of the sort that fills a shelf on its own.

clue.text: Task husband to cut my coiffure, finally (5)

indicators.note: A cut is made into the thing it is made in, so this letter lands inside rather than alongside.
What comes finally comes last, so it is that word's closing letter.

blocks.note: Cor! and My! are the same British exclamation of surprise.
The last letter of coiffure.
H is the standard abbreviation for husband.

annotation.surface: Getting the husband to trim my hair at long last.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My' is the exclamation here — My! and Cor! are the same noise of surprise — not the possessive that the haircut invites. The husband's letter cuts into the middle of it.
annotation.definitionFit: A chore is a small routine task, the dull sort that has to be done rather than chosen.

clue.text: Matter-of-fact drunken tramp with trimmed cigar (9)

indicators.note: A drunk cannot walk in a straight line, and these letters will not keep to their proper order either.
To trim something is to cut a little off its end, so the word loses its last letter.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
The word with its end trimmed off.

annotation.surface: A drunk vagrant holding a cigar with the end cut off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trimmed' works on the cigar in the story and on its letters in the wordplay, taking one off the end. Nine letters out of two ordinary words is a long way to shuffle.
annotation.definitionFit: A pragmatic person deals with things as they actually are, which is what matter-of-fact describes.
